overview: The advantages of batch processing stem from operating over a complete, bounded dataset on a schedule rather than reacting to events one at a time.

Key benefits include very high throughput, cost efficiency from running on cheaper off-peak/spot compute, a simpler programming model, easy reprocessing/replay, and strong consistency over complete datasets.
Batch is also easier to debug, test, and reproduce because inputs are immutable snapshots, and it enables efficient resource optimization by sizing compute precisely to a known data volume.
learningObjectives: Articulate the concrete advantages of batch processing and the mechanism behind each.
Explain why batch is cheaper and higher-throughput than streaming for periodic workloads.
Connect advantages (idempotent reprocessing, consistency, testability) to real interview scenarios.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The advantages of batch processing are the operational, economic, and correctness benefits that arise from processing a finite dataset as a single scheduled unit of work: maximized throughput through bulk operations, reduced cost via off-peak elastic compute, deterministic and reproducible results over immutable inputs, and a simpler programming and testing model than event-by-event stream processing.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine mailing 1,000 letters. Driving to the post office once with all 1,000 (batch) is far cheaper and faster per letter than making 1,000 separate trips (streaming). You also know exactly how much postage you need, you can re-do the whole trip if something goes wrong, and you can count every letter to be sure none is missing. Those are the advantages of batch.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Batch's advantages are why it has dominated data processing since the mainframe era. Bulk processing amortized expensive machine time across many records. MapReduce (2004) industrialized the throughput and fault-tolerance advantages at web scale, and modern Spark/cloud schedulers added elastic, off-peak cost advantages. Even as streaming matured, batch's economics and simplicity kept it the default for analytics and back-office work.

whyItMatters.business: Batch's cost efficiency directly lowers infrastructure spend, and its reproducibility produces auditable, trustworthy numbers for finance and reporting - reducing the cost of errors.
whyItMatters.engineering: A simpler programming model (no watermarks, no continuous state) and immutable inputs make pipelines easier to build, test, and reason about, lowering maintenance burden and on-call load.
whyItMatters.scalability: Bulk operations over partitioned data deliver high throughput, and elastic clusters scale to the dataset then release resources, matching capacity to demand precisely.
whyItMatters.cost: Running heavy jobs during off-peak windows on spot/preemptible instances and tearing clusters down afterward dramatically cuts compute cost versus always-on streaming.
whyItMatters.reliability: Operating over complete, immutable datasets yields strong consistency and idempotent reruns, so failures are recoverable by simply replaying the job.

coreComponents.name: High-Throughput Bulk Engine
coreComponents.definition: A distributed engine that processes the entire dataset in parallel using vectorized, set-based operations.
coreComponents.purpose: To maximize records processed per second by amortizing per-record overhead across the whole batch.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Partitioning, parallel I/O, columnar reads, shuffle management, and efficient aggregations/joins.
coreComponents.examples: Apache Spark, MapReduce, BigQuery, Presto/Trino for batch SQL.

coreComponents.name: Elastic / Off-Peak Compute
coreComponents.definition: On-demand clusters provisioned for a job's runtime, often on spot/preemptible instances during low-demand hours.
coreComponents.purpose: To deliver the cost-efficiency advantage by paying only for the runtime and using the cheapest capacity.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Auto-scaling to data volume, scheduling in off-peak windows, terminating after completion.
coreComponents.examples: EMR/Dataproc transient clusters, Databricks job clusters, Kubernetes spot node pools.

coreComponents.name: Immutable Input Snapshot
coreComponents.definition: A fixed, read-only partition/version of the data that the job consumes.
coreComponents.purpose: To enable the consistency, reproducibility, and easy-replay advantages.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Guarantees the same input yields the same output; supports backfills and idempotent reruns.
coreComponents.examples: A dated S3/Parquet partition, a Delta/Iceberg table snapshot, a database export.

internalWorking: The job reads an immutable, bounded input partition in parallel using columnar formats and partition pruning, maximizing I/O throughput.
Set-based, vectorized transformations operate on large chunks of data at once, amortizing scheduling and serialization overhead per record.
Because the input is a fixed snapshot, intermediate results and the final output are deterministic, enabling identical reruns and easy verification against expected control totals.
On completion the elastic cluster is released; on failure the same job replays against the same input, producing identical idempotent output.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Immutable input snapshot -> Elastic off-peak cluster -> Parallel bulk transform -> Deterministic output -> Cluster released (replay-safe on failure)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A nightly job is scheduled for an off-peak 02:00 window on a transient spot cluster sized to last night's data volume.
2. It reads the immutable daily partition as Parquet, pruning to only needed columns and the single date.
3. Set-based aggregations compute daily metrics in parallel across the cluster at high throughput.
4. Output is written idempotently; the cluster terminates, having incurred cost only for the actual runtime. If it had failed, an identical replay would have produced the same result.

keyTerminology.meaning: The volume of data (records/bytes) processed per unit time.
keyTerminology.importance: Batch maximizes throughput via bulk operations, a primary advantage over per-event streaming.

keyTerminology.meaning: A property where running the operation multiple times yields the same result as running it once.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables safe replay and reprocessing - a core reliability advantage of batch.

keyTerminology.meaning: Cheaper, interruptible compute capacity used during low-demand periods.
keyTerminology.importance: The mechanism behind batch's cost-efficiency advantage.

importantConcepts.explanation: Because batch waits for and processes the entire bounded dataset, aggregates and joins reflect a complete, consistent view - no partial windows or late-event uncertainty as in streaming. This is why control totals reconcile cleanly.

When logic changes or a bug is found, batch lets you simply re-run the job against historical immutable partitions (backfill) to regenerate correct outputs - far simpler than replaying a stream with state.

variationsAndTypes: **Throughput advantage:** Realized by large bulk jobs (Spark/MapReduce) over big partitions.
**Cost advantage:** Realized via transient spot clusters and off-peak scheduling.
**Simplicity/testability advantage:** Realized through deterministic, immutable inputs that make unit and end-to-end testing trivial compared to stateful streaming.
advantages: **High throughput:** Bulk, set-based operations process huge volumes efficiently per unit time.
**Cost efficiency:** Off-peak/spot, right-sized, ephemeral clusters minimize compute spend.
**Simpler programming model:** No watermarks, event-time skew, or continuous state to manage.
**Easy reprocessing/replay:** Backfills and reruns against immutable partitions are straightforward and idempotent.
**Strong consistency:** Complete-dataset processing yields accurate, reconcilable aggregates.
**Easier debugging/testing:** Deterministic inputs make failures reproducible and tests simple.
**Resource optimization:** Compute is sized to a known volume and released after the run.
disadvantages: **High latency:** Outputs are only as fresh as the last completed run.
**Resource spikes:** Concentrated load during the window can strain shared infrastructure.
**Stale data between runs:** Mid-cycle decisions rely on prior-batch data.
**Whole-job failure cost:** A late failure in a big job may require reprocessing all of it.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Lean on batch's advantages when you need maximum throughput at minimum cost, strong consistency over complete data, and easy reprocessing - and the business tolerates minutes-to-hours latency (ETL, billing, reporting, ML training).
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Don't rely on batch when the use case demands sub-second freshness; then streaming's low-latency advantage outweighs batch's cost/throughput benefits, despite added complexity.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Cooking for a dinner party in one big batch is cheaper (buy ingredients in bulk), faster per serving, and easier to get consistent (you season the whole pot once and taste before serving) than cooking each guest's plate to order the moment they arrive. The trade-off is everyone eats at the same scheduled time rather than on demand.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Batch is slower than streaming, so it has no performance advantage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Batch has higher latency but far higher throughput. For moving large volumes of data efficiently, batch is typically faster and cheaper per record than streaming.
Running ephemeral spot clusters in off-peak windows instead of a 24/7 streaming cluster sized for peak can cut compute costs by an order of magnitude for the same periodic workload.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Throughput scales near-linearly by adding workers over partitioned data; elastic clusters expand for the run and contract after, optimizing resource use.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Idempotent reruns over immutable inputs make recovery trivial - replay the job. This is a major reliability advantage for critical financial pipelines.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Lineage-based recomputation (Spark) and orchestrator retries recover from task and node failures without manual intervention.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track throughput (rows/sec), cost per run, runtime vs. SLA, and control-total reconciliation to confirm the advantages are being realized.
productionConsiderations.security: Scoped service accounts, encryption, and audit logs apply; immutable inputs also aid forensic reproducibility.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Spot instances, off-peak scheduling, right-sizing, columnar formats, and caching reference data compound the cost advantage.
productionConsiderations.performance: Partition pruning, predicate pushdown, broadcast joins, and small-file compaction keep bulk jobs fast and cheap.

codeExamples.title: High-Throughput Aggregation Demonstrating Batch Efficiency (PySpark)
codeExamples.overview: A batch job that aggregates a large bounded dataset using set-based operations - showing the throughput and simplicity advantages versus per-event processing.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName("daily_metrics")
    # cost advantage: cluster sized to the run, dynamic allocation releases idle executors
    .config("spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled", "true")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "400")
    .getOrCreate())

run_date = "2026-06-17"

# Throughput advantage: read the whole partition once, columnar + pruned
events = spark.read.parquet(f"s3://events/dt={run_date}").select("user_id", "region", "amount")

# Simplicity advantage: one declarative set-based aggregation, no streaming state
metrics = (events
    .groupBy("region")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"),
         F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("active_users"))
    .withColumn("dt", F.lit(run_date)))

# Reprocessing/consistency advantage: idempotent partition overwrite
(metrics.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("dt")
    .parquet("s3://warehouse/region_metrics"))

spark.stop()
codeExamples.breakdown: Dynamic allocation gives the cost/resource-optimization advantage by releasing idle executors. The single columnar read plus one set-based aggregation gives throughput and simplicity. The idempotent overwrite gives the consistency and easy-replay advantages.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A partition s3://warehouse/region_metrics/dt=2026-06-17 with one row per region (revenue, active_users), produced identically on any rerun.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Over-provisioning executors negates the cost advantage; selecting all columns instead of pruning reduces throughput.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Tune shuffle partitions to data size, enable AQE (adaptive query execution), and use spot instances for the job cluster to maximize the cost advantage.

codeExamples.title: Idempotent Backfill Showing Easy Reprocessing (Bash + Spark)
codeExamples.overview: Re-running a batch job over a range of historical dates to demonstrate the replay/reprocessing advantage after a logic fix.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Reprocessing advantage: replay any historical date range over immutable inputs.
# Each run overwrites only its own partition, so this is fully idempotent.
START="2026-06-01"
END="2026-06-17"

d="$START"
while [[ "$d" < "$END" || "$d" == "$END" ]]; do
  echo "Backfilling $d"
  spark-submit daily_metrics.py "$d"   # same code, different bounded input
  d=$(date -I -d "$d + 1 day")
done

echo "Backfill complete - outputs are byte-identical to a fresh run for each date."
codeExamples.breakdown: Because each run reads an immutable dated partition and overwrites only that output partition, replaying any date range regenerates correct data with no duplicates - the core easy-reprocessing advantage of batch.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Partitions dt=2026-06-01 .. dt=2026-06-17 in the metrics table are regenerated with the new logic, each identical to a single fresh run.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If the job appends instead of overwriting per partition, the backfill creates duplicates and loses idempotency.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Parallelize independent date runs across the cluster, or trigger via Airflow backfill with max_active_runs to control load.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer needs accurate daily sales analytics and wants to minimize cloud spend. Real-time freshness is unnecessary; leadership reviews dashboards each morning.
endToEndExample.inputData: A day's bounded partition of point-of-sale transactions in Parquet on object storage, plus store and product dimension tables.
endToEndExample.architecture: An Airflow-scheduled nightly Spark job runs on a transient spot cluster in an off-peak window. It reads the immutable daily partition, joins dimensions, aggregates sales, and writes idempotent daily fact partitions consumed by BI dashboards.
processingSteps: 1. At 02:00, a transient spot cluster is provisioned, sized to the day's volume.
2. Spark reads the immutable daily transaction partition with column pruning (throughput advantage).
3. Broadcast joins enrich with store/product dimensions; set-based aggregations compute sales metrics.
4. Output is written idempotently to the daily fact partition (consistency + replay advantage).
5. The cluster terminates, incurring cost only for the runtime (cost + resource-optimization advantage).
endToEndExample.output: A complete, reconcilable daily sales fact table powering morning dashboards, produced cheaply and reproducibly.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track throughput (rows/sec), cost per run, runtime vs. the morning SLA, and reconciliation of summed sales against source control totals.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Failures trigger an idempotent rerun against the same immutable partition; no duplicates result, and control-total checks gate dashboard publication.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Trustworthy daily analytics delivered before business hours at a fraction of the cost of a 24/7 streaming pipeline, with effortless backfills when logic changes.

industryUseCases.problem: Producing daily and weekly analytics, recommendation features, and royalty calculations over enormous play-event volumes at controlled cost.
industryUseCases.solution: Large-scale nightly batch jobs (historically MapReduce/Scalding, now Spark/Dataflow) run on elastic clusters over immutable daily partitions.
industryUseCases.benefits: Very high throughput, low cost via elastic compute, reproducible features and royalty figures, and easy backfills when models or rules change.

industryUseCases.problem: Computing pricing, search-ranking features, and financial reporting accurately and cost-effectively across huge datasets.
industryUseCases.solution: Airflow-orchestrated Spark batch pipelines process complete daily datasets and materialize curated tables and ML features.
industryUseCases.benefits: Strong consistency over complete data, simple testable transformations, and cost-efficient scheduled compute - with trivial reprocessing on logic changes.

industryUseCases.problem: Generating end-of-day risk, regulatory, and statement reports that must be exact, auditable, and reproducible.
industryUseCases.solution: Overnight batch jobs process the complete day's bounded data over immutable snapshots and write idempotent outputs.
industryUseCases.benefits: Strong consistency and auditability, idempotent reruns for compliance, and efficient off-peak resource use.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Throughput scales near-linearly by adding executors over partitioned input; clusters auto-scale to the dataset and release resources after, so capacity tracks the known volume precisely.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Spark recomputes lost partitions from lineage and the orchestrator retries failed tasks; idempotent outputs mean any replay is safe - a direct reliability advantage.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Compute is ephemeral, so HA focuses on a highly available orchestrator and metastore; jobs can be relaunched on new clusters with no state to recover.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Immutable inputs and outputs in replicated storage allow full reconstruction by re-running jobs in another region - all derived data is recomputable from source.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Columnar formats, partition pruning, predicate pushdown, broadcast joins, AQE, and small-file compaction maximize throughput while minimizing cost.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Off-peak scheduling, spot/preemptible instances, right-sized transient clusters, dynamic allocation, and cached reference data compound batch's cost advantage.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Least-privilege service accounts, encryption at rest/in transit, PII masking in derived tables, and audit logging; immutable inputs also support forensic reproducibility.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Dashboards for throughput, cost-per-run, runtime vs. SLA, and data-quality control totals confirm the advantages are realized; alerts on regressions.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Complete-dataset processing enables exact control-total and referential checks before publish, leveraging batch's strong-consistency advantage.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Structured logs tagged with run_date and lineage are centralized; alerts on failures, cost spikes, throughput drops, and SLA breaches notify on-call.

recommendedPractices: **Exploit off-peak spot compute:** Schedule heavy jobs in low-demand windows on interruptible instances to realize the cost advantage.
**Keep inputs immutable and outputs idempotent:** This unlocks the replay, consistency, and reliability advantages.
**Use columnar formats and pruning:** Parquet/ORC plus partition pruning maximizes the throughput advantage.
**Validate with control totals:** Leverage complete-dataset consistency to verify correctness before publishing.
engineeringStandards: Jobs must be deterministic given a fixed input to preserve reproducibility and testability.
Outputs must be idempotent (partition overwrite) so reruns/backfills are safe.
Clusters must be right-sized and ephemeral to avoid eroding the cost advantage.
designRecommendations: Partition by date to enable pruning and cheap backfills.
Prefer set-based transformations over row-by-row UDFs to keep throughput high.
Cache or broadcast small reference data to avoid repeated scans.
namingConventions: Name jobs by domain and cadence (e.g., daily_sales_facts).
Use consistent partition keys (dt=YYYY-MM-DD) across datasets.
documentationStandards: Document the schedule, SLA, cost target, and resource sizing for each job.
Capture expected control totals and quality checks per dataset.
testingStrategies: Unit-test transformations on fixed fixtures - deterministic inputs make this easy (a key advantage).
Assert idempotency by running a partition twice and comparing outputs.
Validate throughput and cost regressions in CI/perf tests on sample data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving clusters running 24/7 for a periodic batch job.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams reuse a long-lived cluster for convenience instead of provisioning ephemeral job clusters.
commonMistakes.impact: Erodes the central cost advantage of batch by paying for idle compute around the clock.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use transient, right-sized job clusters on spot capacity that terminate after the run.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing non-idempotent output, defeating the easy-replay advantage.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Append is the default write mode and reruns aren't designed for.
commonMistakes.impact: Backfills and retries create duplicates, undermining the consistency advantage.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Overwrite by partition keyed on run date so every replay is identical.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using row-by-row UDFs/loops instead of set-based operations.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Procedural habits carried over from application code.
commonMistakes.impact: Destroys the throughput advantage and inflates cost and runtime.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Express logic as declarative, vectorized DataFrame/SQL operations the engine can parallelize.

comparisonSection.explanation: Batch maximizes records-per-second through bulk operations, ideal for moving large volumes cheaply. Streaming minimizes latency for immediate action but processes events with more per-record overhead and complexity.

Batch has a simpler model - immutable inputs, deterministic outputs, easy tests and backfills. Streaming must handle watermarks, event-time skew, continuous state, and exactly-once semantics, raising development and operational cost.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main advantages of batch processing?
beginnerQuestions.answer: High throughput from bulk operations, cost efficiency from off-peak/spot elastic compute, a simpler programming model, easy reprocessing/replay via immutable partitions, strong consistency over complete datasets, and easier debugging/testing because inputs are deterministic.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: List the advantages and pair each with its mechanism (bulk ops -> throughput, ephemeral spot -> cost, immutable input -> replay/consistency).

beginnerQuestions.question: Why is batch processing typically cheaper than streaming for periodic workloads?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Batch runs on transient clusters sized to a known volume during off-peak hours on spot/preemptible instances and releases them when done, paying only for runtime. Streaming requires always-on clusters sized for peak, costing far more for the same periodic output.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize ephemeral + right-sized + off-peak/spot vs. 24/7 peak-sized capacity.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does batch give 'strong consistency over complete datasets', and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Batch waits for and processes the entire bounded dataset, so aggregates and joins reflect a complete, consistent snapshot with no partial windows or late-event uncertainty. This matters for billing, reporting, and reconciliation, where totals must be exact and reconcilable.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Contrast with streaming's windowed, late-arrival-prone view. Mention control-total reconciliation as proof of consistency.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is batch easier to debug and test than streaming?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Inputs are immutable snapshots, so runs are deterministic and reproducible: a failure can be replayed exactly, and transformations can be unit-tested against fixed fixtures. Streaming involves continuous state, timing, and event-time effects that are far harder to reproduce.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie determinism and immutable inputs to reproducible failures and simple fixtures.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the throughput advantage of batch at the engine level.
advancedQuestions.answer: Batch reads large partitions with columnar I/O and applies set-based, vectorized operations across many cores/nodes, amortizing scheduling, serialization, and I/O overhead over millions of records. Bulk shuffles and broadcast joins further reduce per-record cost, yielding far higher records-per-second than processing events individually.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show systems-level understanding: vectorization, columnar reads, amortized overhead, parallelism.

advancedQuestions.question: How does batch's easy-replay advantage simplify recovering from a logic bug found in production?
advancedQuestions.answer: Because outputs are idempotent and inputs are immutable dated partitions, you fix the code and re-run a backfill over the affected date range; each run overwrites only its partition, regenerating correct data with no duplicates. In streaming you'd need to replay the source with careful state reset and dedup, which is far harder.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect immutability + idempotency to a concrete backfill-driven recovery story.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your streaming pipeline costs $40k/month but the dashboards it feeds are only reviewed daily. How do you cut cost while keeping correctness?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Match latency to business need (daily), then exploit batch advantages: ephemeral off-peak spot clusters, complete-dataset consistency, idempotent outputs.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Replace streaming with a nightly batch job on transient spot clusters sized to the daily volume. This realizes the cost advantage (pay only for runtime), keeps strong consistency over complete data for accurate dashboards, and adds easy backfills - cutting cost dramatically with no loss the business notices.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a cost-optimized analytics pipeline for daily KPIs over terabytes of event data.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Land immutable daily Parquet partitions in object storage. Run an Airflow-scheduled Spark batch job on transient spot clusters in an off-peak window; use partition pruning, AQE, and broadcast joins for throughput. Write idempotent daily fact partitions consumed by BI.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Gain throughput, cost efficiency, consistency, and easy backfills at the cost of daily-level latency - acceptable for KPIs. If intra-day views are later needed, add micro-batch rather than full streaming.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition by date; auto-scale executors to volume with dynamic allocation; compact small files; backfill via parameterized run dates when logic changes.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Batch's advantages: high throughput, low cost (off-peak/spot), simple model, easy replay/backfill, strong consistency over complete data, and easy testing/debugging via immutable inputs.
keyConcepts: Ephemeral off-peak spot clusters -> low cost.
formulas: Cost savings (rough) = (24/7 peak-sized streaming cost) - (runtime-only right-sized batch cost); the larger the idle fraction streaming covered, the bigger the batch saving.
interviewPoints: Pair each advantage with its mechanism.
Throughput high, latency high - know the trade-off.
Immutable inputs drive consistency, testability, replay.
Idempotency makes recovery and backfills trivial.
quickNotes: Batch is faster per record (throughput) even though it's slower end-to-end (latency).
Always use partition overwrite to keep replay idempotent.
Don't keep job clusters alive - that kills the cost advantage.
Control totals prove the consistency advantage.

keyTakeaways: Batch's headline advantages are high throughput, cost efficiency, a simpler programming model, easy reprocessing/replay, strong consistency over complete datasets, and easier debugging/testing.
The cost advantage comes from running ephemeral, right-sized clusters during off-peak windows on spot/preemptible compute, paying only for runtime versus 24/7 peak-sized streaming.
Immutable inputs make batch deterministic, which simultaneously delivers the reproducibility, testability, and easy-replay advantages.
Processing the complete bounded dataset gives strong consistency, so aggregates reconcile cleanly - critical for billing, reporting, and reconciliation.
Batch trades latency for throughput: it is slower end-to-end but moves large volumes faster and cheaper per record than streaming.
